claims.statement: After the failed Rooke match, Tom Allen issued a challenge to fight any man in the country for $2,500 to $5,000 a side and the championship of the world.
Ben Hogan says he challenged Tom Allen in the summer of 1875 (printed as 'mer of 1875').
In January 1875 George Rooke of Newark, N.J., challenged Tom Allen to fight him for the championship of America for $2,500 a side.
George Rooke, signing himself 'Champion of the United States', issued a challenge to heavyweight fighters, and to Tom Allen in particular.
Tom Allen authorized his friend Arthur Chambers to accept George Rooke's challenge.
Tom Allen and Rooke met at Harry Hill's in New York on 16 February 1875 to discuss the stakes.
According to the New York Sun, Arthur Chambers named Tom Allen as his 'unknown' for a $2,500-a-side match with George Rooke.
A deposit of $500 a side, one-sixth of the agreed stake, was held by Harry Hill for Allen's match with George Rooke.
Ben Hogan of Petrolia, then giving sparring exhibitions in New York, challenged Tom Allen to fight him for $2,500 a side.
Tom Allen accepted Ben Hogan's challenge in a letter from St. Louis to Sam French, saying he would fight Hogan in the same ring on the same day as George Rooke.
Tom Allen told a Democrat reporter at the Champion's Rest that he had received no challenge from Ben Hogan, which the paper called a falsehood.
Tom Allen told the reporter that any match between himself and Ben Hogan was impossible.
Tom Allen sent a $250 deposit to Sam French by Adams Express, received on April 6, 1875, to bind the match.
A club of about sixty sporting men friendly to Allen put up another $250, making $500 for a match with Hogan for an amount printed as $5. OD to $20,000.
Arthur Chambers, acting for Allen, sent articles to Harry Hill's for George Rooke to sign for a fight within fifty miles of Detroit at $1,000 a side.
Allen had sent a telegram to Philadelphia a few days earlier, which was forwarded to Arthur Chambers, and the articles were the response.
In late June 1875 there was talk of a match between Tom Allen and Ned O'Baldwin, and for three months efforts to arrange a meeting were made.
Rooke's backer Muldoon, through Billy Edwards, offered to match Rooke against Allen for $1,000 within ten days, 50 miles from Pittsburg, with Harry Hill as stakeholder.
Rooke challenged Tom Allen to fight without stakes and offered to bet $1,000 that he would whip him.
Teddy Neary, brother of Fiddler Neary, was also eager to fight Rooke and would be matched against him if Allen's challenge came to nothing.
New York rivals spread a report that Tom Allen had challenged Jem Mace and that Mace had accepted; the paper says this was a scheme and not true.

Jem Mace, in a letter dated London, October 27, challenged Allen to fight within fifty miles of Detroit or Pittsburgh for £200 or £1,000 a side (printed as '£1,009'), and asked Allen to deposit $250 with Frank Queen.
Tom Allen telegraphed Mace that he was ready to meet him on Mace's terms, $5,000 a side, and would cover any amount Mace put up.
Tom Allen said there was no truth in the report that he had put up a forfeit for a fight with Jem Mace.
Tom Allen said he had done nothing to bring Jem Mace forward with a challenge and had not heard from Mace in any official manner.
Allen said he would not fight Mace in the East.
Allen said he was by no means loth to meet Mace in a twenty-four foot ring.
Allen was willing to back himself for a sum (unreadable in the OCR) if Mace would fight in the Indian Territory or another Western or Southwestern region.
